source.title: Predicting Machine Translation Performance on Low-Resource Languages: The Role of Domain Similarity
source.authors: Eric Khiu; Hasti Toossi; David Anugraha; Jin-Yu Liu; Jiaxu Li; Juan Armando Parra Flores; Leandro Acros Roman; A. Seza Doğruöz; E. Lee

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, but some table formatting is flattened and Table 4's header-to-value alignment is ambiguous.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses regression and cross-validation to test prediction of MT performance from fine-tuning corpus size, a related but different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on power-law cross-entropy loss, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, parameter-count or compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation. Its own results concern mBART translation spBLEU and predictions from fine-tuning data size and domain similarity.
record.test_reason: It fits a scaling-law function of fine-tuning corpus size (1k–50k sentence pairs) to mBART spBLEU and compares it with linear, polynomial and log fits. Its own results bear on whether downstream performance is predictable from data scale (V6) in a new setting: low-resource MT fine-tuning. It is a weak test: one model, four size values, under two orders of magnitude, and a downstream metric rather than loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude domain similarity is the most important factor in predicting MT spBLEU for these languages, above fine-tuning corpus size and language features. Size-based (scaling-law) prediction works only when in-domain and out-domain data are separated. They call the approach statistically rigorous, while noting limited data and bias toward low spBLEU.
record.recipe_differences: Uses classical regression and cross-validation on MT spBLEU from mBART fine-tuning experiments; it does not measure pretraining cross-entropy, model-parameter scaling, training compute, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction error and residual behavior vary with partitioning; the paper reports differences by fine-tuning/testing corpus and by language, with SI less predictable under the size-based model.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning/test domain similarity (JSD) is the strongest predictor of spBLEU: r=-0.9176, 88% Random Forest importance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain similarity between fine-tuning and test data predicts downstream MT performance better than fine-tuning data size.

record.problems: The study reports only four unique fine-tuning size values, uses a limited set of five South Asian languages and one model, and notes prediction bias toward low spBLEU and heteroscedastic residuals in several partitions. Sinhala uses different corpus versions. The supplied Table 4 layout is flattened and ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: Some Table 4 RMSE cells for alternative size predictors and partition schemes were not extracted because the flattened header-to-cell alignment in the supplied text is ambiguous.

untested.parts: Model-parameter or compute scale, and prediction from pretraining loss. Only fine-tuning data size is varied, for one model (mBART), five South Asian languages, and sizes from 1k to 50k.
All: no pretraining loss is measured.
All: no extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
The fine-tuning regime is studied, but only spBLEU is measured, not loss, so the power-law loss form is not tested.
No exponent or compute-optimal-split comparison across setups.

missing.what: Size-only predictor RMSE under the other partitioning schemes: about 12.8–13.2 with no partition, by fine-tune corpus or by test corpus, and about 11.1–11.3 by language (one poly3 cell reads 22.48). This shows size predicts poorly unless domains are separated.
Pearson correlation of fine-tuning size with spBLEU: r=0.2468, p=0.0010; Random Forest importance 7.8%.
Raw spBLEU rising with fine-tuning size 1k→50k in every column (e.g. TA Gov 21.7→49.5).

record.verdict_notes: The scaling law is one of several regression forms in a performance-prediction study. Its test value for the claim is weak: four sizes spanning under two orders of magnitude, a downstream metric, and fits nearly indistinguishable from log or cubic. The 'out-domain' labels in Section 5.2 conflict with the paper's own in-domain definition.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study does not fit pretraining-loss laws on small runs and test them on substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is studied.
The study does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Although it studies fine-tuned MT, it does not test whether the claimed power-law loss form holds in this regime or in other modalities.
Tests MT spBLEU prediction using fine-tuning corpus size, not model scale or pretraining loss; covers one pretrained model and five South Asian languages.

Compares prediction functions and partitioning for MT spBLEU, but does not test scaling-law exponent or compute-optimal-split dependence on setup, nor systematic departures of loss curves from a power law.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Fit the scaling-law predictor to fine-tuning corpus size and evaluate spBLEU prediction with 10-fold cross-validation.

conditions.value: by both fine-tuning and testing corpora

rows.note: The authors report this as the lowest RMSE for size predictors under the best partitioning scheme. The evaluation predicts MT performance, not pretraining loss.
rows.check: Within the fine-tuning×test partition the size-based scaling law predicts spBLEU well (RMSE 2.2998). The baseline should be the other size predictors on the same partition: linear 2.9682, log 2.3077, poly3 2.3335. The scaling law barely beats the log fit, so the power-law form itself is not distinguished.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Assess residuals from the size-based scaling-law predictor.

conditions.value: scaling law on fine-tuning corpus size

rows.value: Residuals follow a normal distribution on all partitions.
rows.note: This is a residual diagnostic for spBLEU prediction, not a test of a power law in held-out loss.
rows.check: Residual normality is a model diagnostic, not a scaling result. Table 5a gives normality p-values of 0.138–0.613, all above 0.05.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Compare residuals from the size-based scaling-law predictor across fine-tuning and testing corpus partitions.
rows.measure: Residual mean and variance; residual homoscedasticity
rows.baseline: In-domain partitions have higher residual mean and variance.
rows.value: Out-domain partitions have lower residual mean and variance; partitions involving the Bible corpus are heteroscedastic.
rows.note: The authors attribute the lower residuals partly to the narrower spBLEU range out of domain; most out-domain partitions show heteroscedasticity.
rows.check: Table 5a: 4 of 6 partitions are heteroscedastic (bible-FLORES, bible-gov, gov-bible, gov-gov). The paper calls gov-gov and bible-bible 'out-domain', although by its own definition they are in-domain, so the baseline wording is inconsistent.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Compare residuals from the size-based scaling-law predictor across language partitions.

conditions.value: scaling law on fine-tuning corpus size

rows.baseline: Other language partitions are not specified as a numeric baseline.
rows.value: SI has relatively high residual mean and variance.
rows.note: The authors suggest that use of different Bible and FLORES corpus versions for SI contributes to the greater prediction difficulty.
rows.check: Qualitative only: SI residuals are larger under the size scaling law. No number is given.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Assess the size predictor's available fine-tuning corpus-size values.
rows.measure: Number of unique fine-tuning corpus sizes available for prediction
rows.value: There are only four unique size values.
rows.note: The authors identify the limited number of size values as a reason size-based prediction is less favorable in some partitions.
rows.check: This is a property of the dataset (four unique sizes), not a result. It should be a note, not a row.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Predict MT spBLEU from JSD between fine-tuning and testing corpora using degree-3 polynomial regression.
rows.note: This is an outcome for domain-based prediction, which is not among the predictors named in the claim versions.
rows.check: Domain-similarity (JSD) predictor; not a scale measure.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Predict MT spBLEU from JSD between fine-tuning and testing corpora using logarithmic regression.
rows.note: The paper presents this as the best-performing non-polynomial model using JSD.
rows.check: JSD predictor comparison; not a scale measure.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Calculate Pearson correlation between JSD and MT spBLEU.
rows.note: The authors interpret JSD as strongly and significantly correlated with spBLEU; this is a domain-similarity finding rather than a scale/loss result.
rows.check: JSD correlation; not a scale measure.

rows.subject: mBART
rows.operation_detail: Rank features by their importance in a Random Forest regressor predicting MT spBLEU.

conditions.value: JSD between fine-tuning and testing corpora

rows.note: The paper reports JSD as the highest-ranked feature; this does not measure a scaling-law claim.
rows.check: Random Forest feature importance for JSD; not a scale measure.

relationships.condition: mBART EN→XX fine-tuning, data split by fine-tuning×test corpus
relationships.reason: The size scaling law predicts spBLEU with RMSE 2.2998 and normally distributed residuals (R1, R2). Note that log and poly3 fits are nearly as good, so the power-law form is not singled out.
relationships.display_finding: The scaling law predicted spBLEU with RMSE 2.2998 and normally distributed residuals, while logarithmic and cubic fits performed nearly as well.

relationships.reason: Most fine-tuning×test partitions are heteroscedastic (R3) and SI is less predictable (R4). From the text: without domain partitioning, size-based RMSE is about 11–13 (Table 4), so size alone fails across domain shift.
relationships.display_finding: Size-based predictions without domain partitioning had RMSE around 11–13, with unequal error variance across most partitions and less predictable SI performance.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
